public import FormalConjecturesUtil

/-!
# Open questions about Fermat numbers

*Reference:* [Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_number)
-/

@[expose] public section

namespace Fermat

/--
Are Fermat numbers composite for all `n > 4`?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem fermat_number_are_composite : answer(sorry) ↔ ∀ n > 4, ¬Prime n.fermatNumber := by
  sorry

/--
Are there infinitely many Fermat primes?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem infinite_fermat_primes : answer(sorry) ↔ Infinite {n : ℕ | Prime n.fermatNumber} := by
  sorry

/--
Are there infinitely many composite Fermat numbers?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem infinite_fermat_composite : answer(sorry) ↔ Infinite {n : ℕ | ¬Prime n.fermatNumber} := by
  sorry

/--
Does a Fermat number exist that is not square-free?
-/
@[category research open, AMS 11]
theorem exists_fermat_not_squarefree : answer(sorry) ↔ ∃ n : ℕ, ¬Squarefree n.fermatNumber := by
  sorry

end Fermat

reformulations.difference: Lean asks whether infinitely many indices n give a prime Fermat number, rather than directly asserting infinitude of the set of Fermat-prime values.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Nat.fermatNumber is strictly increasing and therefore injective. It bijects the qualifying indices with the Fermat-prime values. Nat.prime_iff identifies the generic Prime predicate with natural-number primality. The exact biconditional is proved as Review.infinite_primes_iff_source in /workspace/review/scratch.lean.

reformulations.difference: Lean counts indices with nonprime Fermat numbers, whereas the source asks for infinitely many distinct composite Fermat numbers.
reformulations.equivalence_argument: Every Fermat number is at least 3, so nonprimality is precisely compositeness, with neither 0 nor 1 an exception. Injectivity of Nat.fermatNumber identifies the qualifying indices with the distinct composite values. The exact biconditional is proved as Review.infinite_composites_iff_source in /workspace/review/scratch.lean.

sources_consulted: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat_number — definition, Primality, and Heuristic arguments sections
review.notes: All four declarations faithfully state the four questions explicitly listed as open in Wikipedia’s Primality section. The quantifier scopes, n > 4 bound, answer polarities, and research-open tags agree. The scratch file compiles without errors or warnings and proves the nonprime/composite, index/value, and squarefree/prime-square-divisor equivalences without sorryAx. Boundary computations verify F₀ through F₄ are prime and square-free, while F₅ = 641 × 6700417 is composite and square-free.
